theory.intro: A fraction only makes sense when you know the whole it refers to. Two fractions can only be compared or added when they describe the **same whole**.
facts: $\tfrac{1}{2}$ of a small pizza is **less** than $\tfrac{1}{2}$ of a large pizza — the wholes differ.
To compare or add fractions, the **whole must be the same size**.
The denominator names how many equal parts the **one whole** is split into.
steps: Identify the whole each fraction refers to.
Check the wholes are the same size.
Only then compare, add or subtract the fractions.

foundation.solution_text:
Mia: $8\div2=4$ cm
Noah: $12\div2=6$ cm
Noah has the longer piece because the wholes differ.

foundation.question_text: A small tray and a large tray each have $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of their area covered. Are the covered areas necessarily equal?
foundation.solution_text:
The wholes are different sizes.
The covered areas are **not necessarily equal**.

foundation.question_text: Lena ate $\tfrac{2}{5}$ of one identical sandwich and Kai ate $\tfrac{3}{5}$ of another. Who ate more?
foundation.solution_text:
$\frac{3}{5}>\frac{2}{5}$
Kai ate more because the sandwiches are the same size.

foundation.question_text: Can $\tfrac{1}{3}$ of a large bottle be compared fairly with $\tfrac{1}{2}$ of a small bottle without knowing their capacities? Explain.
foundation.solution_text:
The fractions refer to different wholes of unknown size.
A fair comparison **cannot be made**.

foundation.question_text: Two equal sheets of paper are used. One has $\tfrac{4}{6}$ coloured and the other has $\tfrac{5}{6}$ coloured. Which coloured area is greater?
foundation.solution_text:
$\frac{5}{6}>\frac{4}{6}$
The second coloured area is greater because the wholes are equal.

foundation.question_text: A recipe uses $\tfrac{1}{4}$ of a $1$ kg bag and $\tfrac{1}{4}$ of a $2$ kg bag. Are the amounts the same?
foundation.solution_text:
$1\div4=0.25$ kg
$2\div4=0.5$ kg
The amounts are different because the whole bags differ.

development.question_text: Ava says, “$\tfrac{3}{8}>\tfrac{2}{8}$, so $\tfrac{3}{8}$ of any object is always larger.” Correct her claim.
development.solution_text:
$\frac{3}{8}>\frac{2}{8}$ only when the wholes are the same size.
Different wholes can reverse the comparison.

development.question_text: Tank A holds $40$ L and is $\tfrac{3}{5}$ full. Tank B holds $60$ L and is $\tfrac{2}{5}$ full. Compare the amounts of water.
development.solution_text:
Tank A: $40\div5\times3=24$ L
Tank B: $60\div5\times2=24$ L
The amounts are equal although the fractions differ.

development.question_text: A $30$ cm strip has $\tfrac{2}{3}$ shaded. A $24$ cm strip has $\tfrac{3}{4}$ shaded. Which shaded length is greater?
development.solution_text:
$30\div3\times2=20$ cm
$24\div4\times3=18$ cm
The first shaded length is greater.

development.question_text: Two classes each say $\tfrac{1}{2}$ of their students brought lunch. Class P has $24$ students and class Q has $30$. How many more students brought lunch in class Q?
development.solution_text:
Class P: $24\div2=12$
Class Q: $30\div2=15$
$15-12=3$
Class Q has $3$ more students.

development.question_text: One square has side length $4$ cm and another has side length $6$ cm. Half of each square is shaded. Compare the shaded areas.
development.solution_text:
Small square: $4\times4\div2=8$ cm$^2$
Large square: $6\times6\div2=18$ cm$^2$
The larger square has $10$ cm$^2$ more shaded.

development.question_text: Ravi adds $\tfrac{1}{3}$ of a jug to $\tfrac{1}{3}$ of a cup and records $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of a jug. Identify the error.
development.solution_text:
The two thirds refer to different wholes.
They cannot be added as $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of one jug.

mastery.question_text: A $48$ L drum is $\tfrac{5}{8}$ full and a $35$ L drum is $\tfrac{6}{7}$ full. Which contains more, and by how much?
mastery.solution_text:
$48\div8\times5=30$ L
$35\div7\times6=30$ L
They contain equal amounts, so the difference is $0$ L.

mastery.question_text: Sam says $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of a whole is greater than $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of a whole. Give whole sizes that make Sam correct.
mastery.solution_text:
Choose wholes of $12$ and $8$.
$\frac{2}{3}$ of $12=8$
$\frac{3}{4}$ of $8=6$
Thus $8>6$, so Sam can be correct when the wholes differ.

mastery.question_text: Box A has $\tfrac{3}{5}$ of its capacity filled and box B has $\tfrac{4}{5}$ filled. Box A contains more. What must be true about the capacities?
mastery.solution_text:
Although $\frac{3}{5}<\frac{4}{5}$, box A contains more.
Box A must have the larger capacity.
